missions/moravian-mission/name: Moravian missions (Herrnhut, Zinzendorf, Dober, Greenland, Caribbean, Suriname)
missions/moravian-mission/statusNote: The Moravian Church (Unitas Fratrum) continues as a worldwide communion of about a million members organised in self-governing provinces; the former mission fields now far outnumber the European and North American provinces, with the largest churches in Tanzania, the Caribbean, Suriname, South Africa and Nicaragua.
missions/moravian-mission/summary: The first Protestant church to treat world mission as the task of the whole community. From the refugee settlement of Herrnhut on Count Zinzendorf's estate, lay artisans went out from 1732 to the enslaved Africans of the Danish West Indies, to Greenland, Suriname, South Africa, Native North America, Labrador, Jamaica and Antigua and eventually to Tibet, Australia, Nicaragua and East Africa. Preaching the suffering Saviour and supporting themselves by their trades, they built enduring Afro-Caribbean and Indigenous churches, while also accepting, and in places practising, slaveholding.
missions/moravian-mission/story:
Herrnhut was founded in 1722 by Protestant refugees from Moravia, some descended from the old Unity of the Brethren (Unitas Fratrum), who settled on the Berthelsdorf estate of Count Nicolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf. After a eucharistic experience of reconciliation on 13 August 1727 the community organised itself into 'choirs', adopted a round-the-clock prayer watch that continued for about a hundred years, and developed an intense devotion to the wounded Lamb of God. Zinzendorf, raised in Halle Pietism, had as a schoolboy formed the 'Order of the Mustard Seed' to spread the gospel and had met the Tranquebar missionary Ziegenbalg.

In 1731, at the coronation of Christian VI in Copenhagen, Zinzendorf's servants met Anthony Ulrich, an enslaved man from the Danish island of St Thomas, and saw Inuit converts of Hans Egede's Greenland mission. Anthony's appeal moved two young men at Herrnhut: Leonhard Dober, a potter, and David Nitschmann, a carpenter. They left Herrnhut on 21 August 1732, walked to Copenhagen and arrived at St Thomas on 13 December 1732. The popular story that they meant to sell themselves into slavery rests on Dober's stated willingness to do so; it never happened. In 1733 Christian David and the cousins Matthäus and Christian Stach went to Greenland, where the first convert, Kajarnak, was baptised in 1739 and the settlement of Neu-Herrnhut grew beside Egede's Godthåb.

Within a decade the small community had sent workers to Suriname (1735), Georgia (1735), the Gold Coast and South Africa (1737), Lapland, Ceylon and the Arctic. On St Thomas the Afro-Caribbean freedwoman Rebecca Protten became a leading evangelist among the enslaved, and when she, her husband Matthäus Freundlich and others were imprisoned in 1738, Zinzendorf himself sailed to the island in 1739 to secure their release. In South Africa Georg Schmidt baptised Khoikhoi converts at Baviaanskloof from 1737 but was forced out in 1744 by Dutch Reformed clergy who disputed a lay missionary's right to baptise; the Moravians returned in 1792 and refounded the station as Genadendal. Antigua (1756) and Jamaica (1754) became major fields, and by the early nineteenth century Moravian congregations in the British and Danish Caribbean counted tens of thousands of members.

In North America the Moravians founded Bethlehem and Nazareth in Pennsylvania (1741) and Salem in North Carolina (1766), and from Shekomeko in New York (1740) built a Christian community among the Mahican and Lenape. David Zeisberger led Christian Lenape through repeated forced migrations to the Ohio country (Schoenbrunn and Gnadenhütten, 1772), where on 8 March 1782 Pennsylvania militia murdered 96 unarmed Christian Lenape men, women and children at Gnadenhütten. From 1771 the Brethren worked among the Inuit of Labrador at Nain, Okak and Hopedale.

The movement's distinctive methods impressed Protestants everywhere. Missionaries were usually craftsmen who earned their keep; they sought 'first-fruits' (individual converts gathered into disciplined settlements) rather than whole nations; they preached the blood and wounds of Christ before teaching about God the Creator; and decisions, including marriages and postings, were often made by lot. John Wesley met Moravians on his 1735 voyage to Georgia and was guided by Peter Böhler before his Aldersgate experience in 1738, and William Carey's Enquiry (1792) held up 'what these Moravians have done' as a rebuke to other churches. The British Society for the Furtherance of the Gospel (1741) supported the work from London.

Crises were frequent: the 'Sifting Time' of the 1740s brought extravagant devotional excess to Herrnhaag; Zinzendorf's debts nearly bankrupted the Unity in the 1750s; and after his death in 1760 the church became more cautious and institutional. Yet the missions kept spreading: to the Mosquito Coast of Nicaragua (1849), Victoria in Australia (1850), the Himalayas at Kyelang (1853) and Leh, where Heinrich August Jäschke compiled a Tibetan dictionary, Alaska (1885) and German East Africa (1891), today Tanzania. Emancipation in the Caribbean (1834–38) and Suriname (1863) transformed the plantation congregations into free churches, and in the twentieth century the provinces became autonomous members of a worldwide Unity governed by a Unity Synod.
missions/moravian-mission/beliefs/0: A 'theology of the heart' centred on the crucified Saviour, the Lamb whose blood and wounds bring salvation, expressed in hymns, litanies and daily texts (the Losungen, from 1731).
missions/moravian-mission/beliefs/1: Conviction that the Holy Spirit was already preparing individuals among all peoples, so that missionaries should seek these 'first-fruits' rather than mass conversions.
missions/moravian-mission/beliefs/2: Acceptance of the Augsburg Confession alongside a broadly ecumenical vision of the 'Unity of the Brethren' as a fellowship within and across churches.
missions/moravian-mission/beliefs/3: Belief that the risen Christ is Chief Elder of the church (declared in 1741) and that his will could be discerned through prayer and the lot.
missions/moravian-mission/beliefs/4: A spiritual, inward equality of believers that coexisted with acceptance of social hierarchy, including slavery, in this world.
missions/moravian-mission/strategies/0: Sending lay artisans (potters, carpenters, weavers) who supported themselves by trade and lived among the people.
missions/moravian-mission/strategies/1: Building disciplined Christian settlements (Neu-Herrnhut, Genadendal, Gnadenhütten, Nain) on the Herrnhut model, with choirs, schools and crafts.
missions/moravian-mission/strategies/2: Learning local languages and creoles, including Dutch Creole on St Thomas, Sranan in Suriname, Greenlandic, Inuktitut, Lenape and Miskito.
missions/moravian-mission/strategies/3: Training and appointing Black and Indigenous 'helpers' and elders, such as Rebecca Protten on St Thomas and the Lenape helpers in Ohio.
missions/moravian-mission/strategies/4: Intensive communication through diaries and reports circulated to all settlements (the Gemeinnachrichten), fostering a global church identity.
missions/moravian-mission/strategies/5: Long-term commitment: missionaries often served for life and were buried in mission graveyards (God's Acres).
missions/moravian-mission/groupsReached/: Enslaved Africans and free people of colour in the Danish West Indies, Jamaica, Antigua, Barbados, St Kitts, Tobago and Suriname.
Khoikhoi and other peoples of the Cape (Genadendal, Elim, Mamre).
Mahican, Lenape (Delaware) and Cherokee communities in North America.
Miskito and other Caribbean coast peoples of Nicaragua and Honduras.
Nyakyusa, Safwa and other peoples of south-western Tanzania; Ladakhi and Lahauli Buddhists in the western Himalayas; Aboriginal Australians in Victoria and Queensland.
missions/moravian-mission/challenges/0: Extremely high mortality in the tropics: dozens of early missionaries to St Thomas, St Croix and Guinea died within months.
missions/moravian-mission/challenges/1: Opposition from planters, colonial clergy and governments, who feared literacy and Christian fellowship among the enslaved.
missions/moravian-mission/challenges/2: Persecution in Europe and America: the Brethren were expelled from Saxony (Zinzendorf exiled 1736–47) and suspected as papists, enthusiasts or French agents in the colonies.
missions/moravian-mission/challenges/3: Frontier violence in North America, culminating in the Gnadenhütten massacre of 1782.
missions/moravian-mission/challenges/4: Financial crisis in the 1750s caused by Zinzendorf's ambitious spending.
missions/moravian-mission/challenges/5: Very small home base: a church of a few thousand members sustained missions on several continents.
missions/moravian-mission/harms/0: The Moravians accepted slavery as an earthly order and preached obedience to masters; the mission itself owned enslaved people on St Thomas, in Suriname and at Salem in North Carolina.
missions/moravian-mission/harms/1: Segregation and racial hierarchy in Moravian congregations, for example the segregated Salem congregation from the 1820s, contradicted their earlier mixed fellowship.
missions/moravian-mission/harms/2: Closed mission settlements imposed detailed rules on Indigenous life and made converts dependent on mission land and trade.
missions/moravian-mission/harms/3: In Greenland and Labrador the trading and settlement systems promoted by missions disrupted Inuit subsistence patterns and exposed communities to epidemic disease.
missions/moravian-mission/harms/4: Moravian-run Aboriginal stations in Australia, such as Ebenezer and Ramahyuck, were part of the protection system that removed Aboriginal people from their land.
missions/moravian-mission/developments/0: The first sustained Protestant mission to enslaved Africans, which helped create Afro-Caribbean Christianity and Black church leadership.
missions/moravian-mission/developments/1: The model of a whole church committed to mission; by the late eighteenth century the Moravians sent proportionally far more missionaries than any other Protestant body.
missions/moravian-mission/developments/2: Linguistic work in Greenlandic, Inuktitut, Sranan, Miskito, Lenape and Tibetan, including Jäschke's Tibetan dictionary (1881).
missions/moravian-mission/developments/3: Schools and teacher-training in the Caribbean and South Africa (Genadendal's teachers' college, 1838) that educated generations of free people of colour.
missions/moravian-mission/developments/4: Decisive influence on John Wesley, William Carey and the British missionary societies of the 1790s.
missions/moravian-mission/developments/5: Self-governing provinces today in Tanzania, the Caribbean, Suriname, South Africa, Nicaragua, Labrador, Alaska and elsewhere.
missions/moravian-mission/outcome: From a refugee village of a few hundred people the Moravian missions produced a worldwide church whose members are now overwhelmingly African, Afro-Caribbean, Latin American and Indigenous. Their example of lay, self-supporting, lifelong mission and their influence on Wesley and Carey make them a hinge between Pietism and the modern Protestant missionary movement, while their accommodation of slavery remains a contested part of the record.
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/0/ro: Patron, bishop and leader of the renewed Unity
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/0/fo: Organising Herrnhut, sending the first missionaries, visiting St Thomas (1739) and Pennsylvania (1741–43)
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/0/ou: Shaped Moravian theology and mission strategy; died at Herrnhut

missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/1/fo: Ministry among enslaved Africans on St Thomas (1732–34)
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/1/ou: Later general elder of the Unity
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/2/ro: Carpenter, missionary and first bishop of the renewed Unity (1735)
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/2/fo: Accompanying Dober to St Thomas; later leading parties to Georgia and Pennsylvania
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/4/fo: Preaching to and leading enslaved women on St Thomas
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/4/ou: Later worked at Herrnhut and on the Gold Coast; died at Christiansborg
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/5/ro: First Protestant missionary in South Africa
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/5/fo: Mission to the Khoikhoi at Baviaanskloof (1737–44)
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/5/ou: Forced out over his baptisms; the station was refounded as Genadendal in 1792
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/6/fo: Organising Moravian settlements and missions in Georgia, Pennsylvania and North Carolina
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/6/ou: Led the Unity after Zinzendorf's death
missions/moravian-mission/keyPeople/7/fo: Christian Lenape towns in Pennsylvania and Ohio; Lenape grammar and hymns

missions/moravian-mission/countries/0/co: Danish West Indies (St Thomas, St Croix, St John)
missions/moravian-mission/countries/0/te: First Moravian mission: Dober and Nitschmann on St Thomas, followed by congregations of thousands of enslaved Africans on all three islands.
missions/moravian-mission/countries/1/te: Neu-Herrnhut beside Godthåb (Nuuk) and later stations; transferred to the Danish Lutheran church in 1900.
missions/moravian-mission/countries/2/te: Work among enslaved Africans in Paramaribo and the plantations and among Maroons (Saramaka, from 1765); now one of the largest Moravian provinces.
missions/moravian-mission/countries/3/te: Georg Schmidt at Baviaanskloof (1737–44); Genadendal refounded 1792, followed by Mamre, Elim and Eastern Cape stations.
missions/moravian-mission/countries/4/te: Settlements at Bethlehem, Nazareth and Salem and missions to Mahican, Lenape and Cherokee peoples.
missions/moravian-mission/countries/5/te: Mission on the estates of absentee planters; Moravian schools and congregations grew rapidly after emancipation.
missions/moravian-mission/countries/6/te: One of the largest early fields, with thousands of members by 1800 and a strong tradition of Black lay leadership.
missions/moravian-mission/countries/7/te: Jens Haven founded Nain among the Inuit; Okak, Hopedale and Hebron followed.
missions/moravian-mission/countries/8/te: Mission among the Miskito and Creole population of Bluefields and Puerto Cabezas; revival in the 1880s made it a major province.
missions/moravian-mission/countries/9/te: Mission at Kyelang (1853) and Leh (1885) in the western Himalayas, with Tibetan translation work by Jäschke.
missions/moravian-mission/countries/10/t: Stations among Aboriginal people at Ebenezer (1859) and Ramahyuck in Victoria and later in Queensland.
missions/moravian-mission/countries/11/t: Mission in the Nyasa (Rungwe) region from 1891 and later in Unyamwezi; today the largest Moravian membership in the world.
missions/moravian-mission/countries/12/t: Mission among the Yup'ik of the Kuskokwim region from Bethel.
missions/moravian-mission/journeys/0/tit: Dober and Nitschmann to St Thomas (1732)
missions/moravian-mission/journeys/0/tex: Setting out on foot from Herrnhut on 21 August 1732 with little money, the two men walked to Copenhagen, where court officials helped them obtain passage on a Dutch ship that sailed on 8 October and reached St Thomas on 13 December 1732. Nitschmann returned in 1733; Dober stayed until 1734.
missions/moravian-mission/journeys/1/tit: The first Moravian party to Greenland (1733)
missions/moravian-mission/journeys/1/peo: Christian David, Matthäus Stach and Christian Stach
missions/moravian-mission/journeys/1/tex: The party sailed from Copenhagen with royal permission and landed near Egede's colony in May 1733, founding Neu-Herrnhut. Years of failure ended when Kajarnak, a southern Greenlander, responded to Johann Beck's reading of the passion narrative in 1738 and was baptised in 1739.
missions/moravian-mission/journeys/2/tex: Arriving in January 1739 to find the missionaries Friedrich Martin and Matthäus and Rebecca Freundlich in prison, Zinzendorf secured their release, preached to large gatherings of enslaved people and, in a notorious sermon, urged them to obey their masters.
missions/moravian-mission/journeys/3/tex: Sent with the support of Dutch Pietists, Schmidt reached the Cape in July 1737 and settled among the Khoikhoi in the Baviaanskloof valley, teaching, farming and eventually baptising five converts, which led to his recall in 1744.
missions/moravian-mission/journeys/4/tit: Zeisberger and the Christian Lenape migrate to Ohio (1772–1782)
missions/moravian-mission/journeys/4/peo: David Zeisberger, John Heckewelder and Christian Lenape
missions/moravian-mission/journeys/4/tex: Pressed by settlers, the Christian Lenape moved from Pennsylvania to the Tuscarawas valley, founding Schoenbrunn and Gnadenhütten. During the Revolutionary War British-allied forces removed them to Sandusky; a group returned to harvest their crops and were massacred by Pennsylvania militia on 8 March 1782.
missions/moravian-mission/relations/0/te: Moravians shaped John Wesley through his voyage to Georgia (1735–36), Peter Böhler's counsel and the Fetter Lane society, and Wesley's visit to Herrnhut in 1738.
missions/moravian-mission/relations/1/te: Carey's Enquiry (1792) cited the Moravians as the model of a small church in earnest about mission, and their Periodical Accounts were read at the BMS's founding meeting.
missions/moravian-mission/relations/2/te: Moravian reports, promoted by the London Society for the Furtherance of the Gospel, helped inspire the evangelicals who founded the LMS in 1795.
missions/moravian-mission/agreements/0/t: Both stressed felt assurance of salvation, small-group discipline and hymn-singing, and both went to the enslaved Caribbean early.
missions/moravian-mission/agreements/1/t: Both drew on Halle Pietism and the Danish crown's colonies, and both prized translation and lifelong service.
missions/moravian-mission/disagreements/: In 1740 Wesley broke with the Fetter Lane Moravians over 'stillness' (waiting for faith without using the means of grace) and later criticised Zinzendorf's antinomian tendencies.
Halle Pietists, especially Gotthilf August Francke, distrusted Zinzendorf's theology and independence and opposed Moravian work in Halle's sphere, including in India (the Nicobar mission of 1768–87).
missions/moravian-mission/deviations/0: The 'Sifting Time' (c. 1743–50) introduced extravagant blood-and-wounds devotion and spiritual excesses that Zinzendorf himself eventually condemned.
missions/moravian-mission/deviations/1: Early mixed-race fellowship on St Thomas and at Bethlehem gave way in the nineteenth century to segregated congregations in the American South.
missions/moravian-mission/deviations/2: From preaching spiritual equality the mission moved to owning enslaved people on its own plantations, contrary to the egalitarian impulse of its origins.
